title: Counted once, even when sent twice
summary: A phone's outbox retries until the server says yes, so the same operation can arrive more than once. Every operation has a unique id, and the merge keeps one copy per id.

predict.prompt: Predict the merged result of your own cases. The real merge then runs on the same operations and checks you; a wrong case is replaced by a new one with different numbers.

cases.template: Phone A received {v0} blankets. The signal dropped and the outbox sent it again. Phone B received {v2}. What is the blanket count?
cases.prompt: Phone A received 10 blankets. The signal dropped and the outbox sent it again. Phone B received 5. What is the blanket count?
cases.question: What is the quantity of blankets?

cases.template: {v0} bags of rice arrive, then one issue of {v1} bags is retried three times. How much rice is left?
cases.prompt: 20 bags of rice arrive, then one issue of 4 bags is retried three times. How much rice is left?
cases.question: What is the quantity of rice?

cases.template: Two copies of id ph-a:1 disagree: one says +{v0} at Lamport {l0}, the other +{v1} at Lamport {l1}. The merge keeps the copy with the larger (lamport, replica, kind, item, value). What is the water count?
cases.prompt: Two copies of id ph-a:1 disagree: one says +4 at Lamport 1, the other +7 at Lamport 2. The merge keeps the copy with the larger (lamport, replica, kind, item, value). What is the water count?
cases.question: What is the quantity of water?

bug.prompt: This merge was changed by one line. Phones now report too many blankets after a bad signal day. What is wrong?

options.text: The quantity sum ignores negative adjustments.
merge groups the raw operations without calling dedupe(), so a retried operation is counted again.
Items are sorted by name, so the delivery order changes the result.

bug.explanation: Without dedupe() every retried copy of an operation is added again. The real merge loops over dedupe(ops), which keeps exactly one operation per id.

write.prompt: Write dedupe(ops): keep one operation per id.
write.stub:
def dedupe(ops):
    """Return each operation exactly once, sorted by id.

    ops is an iterable of Op(id, replica, lamport, kind, item, value). The same id can
    arrive many times. Keep one op per id. If two ops share an id but differ in content,
    keep the one with the larger _total(op), so every phone picks the same copy.
    Call _validate(op) on every op first: it raises ValueError for a malformed op.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError

guided.prompt: Pick the body that does what the docstring says. It is graded by running it, like any other answer.

explain.prompt: In your own words: why can the same operation arrive more than once, and why is it never counted twice? Write at least 25 words, one sentence for each point you make, and use the numbers of your own case p1 as a worked example.

rubric.point: Every operation carries a unique id.
Retries on a flaky network deliver the same operation more than once, so counting every copy gives the wrong total (show it with the numbers of your case).
The merge keeps one operation per id before counting.
So the result is the same however many times and in whatever order operations arrive.

title: Quantity is a sum of signed changes
summary: Phones never send 'the count is 30'. They send changes: +50 received, -12 issued. The quantity is the sum of every signed adjustment, so offline changes from many phones add up.

predict.prompt: Predict the merged result of your own cases. The real merge then runs on the same operations and checks you; a wrong case is replaced by a new one with different numbers.

cases.question: What is the quantity of paracetamol?

    ops is every operation of one item, of any kind ("adjust", "create", "note",

    non-zero int (+ received, - issued). Return the sum of those values.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError

explain.prompt: In your own words: why does the ledger add up signed changes instead of storing the current count? Write at least 25 words, one sentence for each point you make, and use the numbers of your own case p1 as a worked example.

rubric.point: Each operation is a signed change, not an absolute count (show it with the numbers of your case).
Addition gives the same total in any order.
Storing a total would let one phone overwrite another's changes.
Changes made on several phones while offline all count.

title: Last writer wins, by Lamport time
summary: Names, notes and deletions keep one value. The write with the highest (Lamport time, replica id) wins. The phone's wall clock is never used: it can be hours wrong.

predict.prompt: Predict the merged result of your own cases. The real merge then runs on the same operations and checks you; a wrong case is replaced by a new one with different numbers.
